newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Tirana calm, Albanians turn to bingo for cash.
newsitem.headline: Tirana calm, Albanians turn to bingo for cash.

text.p: Calm returned to the streets of Albania's capital on Monday after a big weekend demonstration by angry investors desperate to retrieve their life savings from crumbling get-rich-quick pyramid schemes.

Thousands of demonstrators, led by opposition leaders, stormed through police cordons on Sunday to reach Tirana's main Skanderbeg Square, scene of a 1990 uprising that toppled the former hardline communist regime.

The protesters blamed the conservative government of President Sali Berisha for doing little to regulate the pyramid schemes which promised untold wealth from small investments and have wiped out the life savings of thousands of Albanians.
As pessimism spread through the impoverished Balkan nation, many disillusioned Albanians who had lost all their savings turned to another hope of easy quick money -- television bingo.
Albanians rushed to kiosks on Monday to buy Tele-bingo tickets for half a dollar per game for a possible jackpot of 7.5 million leks (about $75,000).
"I lost all the money I had deposited into Sude's company, and Tele-bingo is my last chance," said a woman after buying some 30 tickets at a kiosk.
The Sude pyramid scheme, once one of the most popular, collapsed last week.
Opposition parties vowed on Sunday to hold fresh protests against Berisha's government but the Interior Ministry warned against illegal demonstrations.

The ministry rejected eyewitness reports that some protesters in Tirana had been hurt in scuffles with police and accused the opposition of encouraging people to daub themselves with red ink in order to fake injury.
The police presence was sparse on Monday morning, with just a few stationed on Tirana's streets and around the central Skanderbeg Square.
"No need for us to politicise this important issue. We protest only to get back our money," a middle-aged man said in a Tirana bar.
"It's good that people protest because the government should take care of us and of our lives -- which could be completely destroyed for thousands of families," a woman said.
Berisha vowed at the weekend to crack down on the pyramid schemes but warned the opposition against exploiting anger among investors to try to destabilise the ex-communist state.

He said his government had respected the citizens' democratic right to give and take money on credit but had in no case allowed state institutions to get involved as has happened in other ex-communist states.
"But we...are determined to crack down on every pyramid scheme, every cheating of the citizen, and are determined to establish all the necessary rules and laws to prevent them," he said.
The government last Thursday ordered the seizure of some 25.5 billion leks ($255 million) deposited by investment schemes in the country's commercial banks.
